Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved

A full treatment: the measurement, the queueing mathematics underneath it, the schools that disagree about what to do with the answer, and the places where the whole frame misleads.

1. Two rooms, one problem

On Tuesday, 10 February 2026, Rhea Kulkarni sat in Sampada Wealth's office in Lower Parel, Mumbai, with a slide she had been asked to defend. Sampada was a consumer investing app: mutual funds, a small direct-equity business, and a goal-planning layer that had become its differentiator. It had 31 lakh registered users, 6.4 lakh who transacted in a typical month, and ₹214 crore of annualised revenue, mostly from distribution commissions and a ₹399-a-year premium tier. Zerodha, Groww and Paytm Money were the reference points in every board conversation; SEBI was the reference point in every legal one.

Sampada's engineering organisation of 96 people had adopted AI coding assistants across the whole team in April 2025. By January 2026 the measured effects were unambiguous in one direction: the median time from the first line of code on a change to the moment that change was ready for review had fallen from 7.2 working days to 2.1. Pull requests merged per week had risen from 41 to 88. Rhea's slide, however, was about the year's goals, and it said that of eleven planned launches, three had reached all users, five were partially rolled out, and three had not begun. The board member who had asked for the slide, a former banker, had written a single line in the margin: where did the 5 days go?

Two thousand kilometres away and four hours earlier in the working day, Devendra Rao — Dev to everyone — was asking a similar question in a different shape at Neelambar Freight Cloud in Baner, Pune. Neelambar sold a transport management system to large shippers and third-party logistics providers: indent-to-delivery workflow, e-way bill integration, freight reconciliation against GST invoices, and a carrier marketplace layer. It had 190 enterprise customers, including two large FMCG manufacturers and a Dubai-based freight forwarder that represented ₹11 crore of annual contract value on its own. Neelambar's team was scattered: 44 engineers in Pune and Bengaluru, a design lead in Berlin, a data scientist in Toronto, a customer-success head in Singapore, and a sales head in New Jersey who sold into North American shippers.

Dev's numbers looked like Rhea's, but his constraint did not. Neelambar's engineers had also cut build time by two-thirds. Its release calendar had not moved at all, because its largest customers did not accept releases on Neelambar's schedule. The Dubai forwarder ran a user-acceptance test cycle that took eleven working days and could only begin after the customer's own IT team scheduled it, which happened on the first and third Monday of each month. Dev had been asked by his CEO to commit to a 2026 roadmap with 40% more scope, on the reasoning that engineering was now 40% more productive. He believed that commitment would fail, and he needed to explain why in terms that were not defensive.

Both are facing the same underlying phenomenon and will need different remedies. That divergence — same diagnosis, different treatment — is the argument this page builds.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

A velocity illusion is the systematic divergence between a team's throughput — items finished per unit time — and its cycle time, the calendar duration from the moment an idea is committed to until its effect on a customer is known. Throughput is a rate; cycle time is a duration; they are related but not interchangeable, and the relation is Little's Law: average work in progress equals average throughput times average cycle time. If throughput doubles and cycle time holds, work in progress has doubled — twice as many unfinished things aging in the system.

The third quantity that makes the phenomenon legible is flow efficiency: the share of an item's cycle time during which someone is actually working on it. Measured honestly in product organisations it typically lands between 5% and 20%. Generative coding tools attack the numerator of that fraction. The denominator is mostly made of waiting.

The lineage runs through three bodies of work. Eliyahu Goldratt's The Goal (1984) and the Theory of Constraints established that a system of dependent steps produces at the rate of its slowest step, and that local improvements elsewhere generate inventory, not output. Donald Reinertsen's The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) imported queueing theory into product development and made two claims that remain the sharpest in the field: that the dominant cost in knowledge work is the cost of queues, which are invisible because half-finished designs do not occupy floor space; and that batch size, not effort, is the primary lever on cycle time. Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim's Accelerate (2018) provided the empirical backbone through the DORA programme, showing that deployment frequency, lead time for change, change-failure rate and time-to-restore move together in high-performing organisations rather than trading off.

What AI added, from roughly 2023 onward, was a large and uneven shock to one stage. That is precisely the condition under which Goldratt's and Reinertsen's results become visible to non-specialists. Four schools now give materially different advice about what to do next, and a manager who cannot distinguish them will accept whichever consultant arrives first.

3. Mechanics in depth

The expert version of this exercise has six steps. Steps two, four and six are the ones usually skipped.

Define the cycle by its economic endpoints, not by tool boundaries. Engineering platforms measure commit-to-deploy because those timestamps are free. That window excludes the decision that precedes the work and the rollout and measurement that follow it — which is to say, it excludes exactly the stages that product managers control and that AI did not touch. Rhea defined Sampada's cycle from plan acceptance to "serving 100% of eligible users with the primary metric read"; Dev defined Neelambar's from plan acceptance to "accepted by the customer in production", because for him the customer's acceptance test is inside the cycle and outside his control.

Instrument the seams, not the stages. The time you are hunting lives in handoffs, and handoffs are usually the boundary between two teams with different managers. A stage boundary is only useful if a system already writes a timestamp there, or can be made to this month. Anything unmeasured becomes the reservoir into which released time silently flows.

Report distributions, and report them per class of work. Median and 85th percentile at minimum. Mixing classes is the most common analytical error: at Neelambar, internal-only changes had a median cycle of 9 days and customer-visible workflow changes a median of 34, and the pooled median of 19 described nothing that existed.

Separate wait time from touch time inside each stage. This is the step that converts an interesting chart into an actionable one. A review stage of six days made of 5.7 days waiting and 0.3 days reading is a capacity-and-batch problem. A review stage of six days made of 1 day waiting and 5 days reading is a comprehension problem, and adding reviewers will not fix it.

Classify each slow stage as a queue, a hard task, or a calendar. Queues respond to capacity and batch size; hard tasks respond to redesign, tooling and scope reduction; calendars respond only to changing the calendar. Dev's eleven-day Dubai acceptance test that starts on alternate Mondays is a calendar wrapped around a hard task, and the average wait it imposes before starting is half of a fortnight — five working days — regardless of anything Neelambar does.

Apply the arithmetic before spending anything. Three formulas carry most of the load.

Amdahl's Law bounds the prize. If a stage occupies fraction f of the cycle and becomes k times faster, overall speed-up is 1 ÷ ((1−f) + f/k). At Sampada, build was 7.2 of a 38-day median cycle, so f = 0.19. Even with k = ∞, the cycle floor is 30.8 days — a 19% improvement, available once and never again from that lever.

Kingman's approximation explains why the released time vanished. For a single-server queue, expected waiting time is approximately (ca² + cs²) ÷ 2 × ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) × te, where ρ is utilisation, te is mean service time, and the c terms are coefficients of variation in arrivals and service. The practical reading has three parts. Wait grows without bound as ρ approaches 1. Wait is proportional to variability, so making work more uniform is as powerful as adding capacity. And AI tooling raises both ρ (more arrivals) and cs (more variable review difficulty, since a 40-line hand-written fix and a 700-line generated refactor now arrive in the same queue), so its effect on waiting is multiplicative, not additive.

Sample-size arithmetic bounds the read stage. To detect a relative lift of r on a baseline conversion p with conventional power, you need roughly 16 × p(1−p) ÷ (rp)² users per arm. At Sampada's 8.3% baseline for the goal-planning flow and a target 3% relative lift, that is about 16 × 0.076 ÷ (0.0025)² ≈ 1.95 lakh users per arm. With 6.4 lakh monthly transactors and only 30% eligible for that surface, a two-arm test needs about four weeks of exposure. No coding assistant shortens it.

The second-order effects deserve naming because they are what make this problem self-reinforcing rather than self-correcting. Higher arrival rates raise work in progress, which raises context-switching, which lowers effective review capacity, which raises ρ further. Longer review queues age branches, which forces rebases, which creates new work that arrives back at the same queue. Reviewers under load approve more shallowly, which raises change-failure rate, which consumes senior attention in incident response — drawn from the same pool of people who do reviews. Each of these loops has a gain slightly less than one in a healthy organisation and slightly more than one in a stressed one, which is why teams describe the transition as sudden.

4. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Stated as testable claims, the frame applies when four conditions hold.

Claim one: the cycle is a chain of dependent stages with observable handoffs. True at both companies. Sampada's chain is plan → build → review → compliance review → release → ramp → read. Neelambar's is plan → build → review → internal verification → customer UAT → production acceptance. Where work is genuinely parallel and independent — a portfolio of unrelated bets with no shared resource — constraint thinking gives poor advice.

Claim two: one stage is materially slower than the others. True at Neelambar, where customer UAT plus its scheduling wait is 16 of 34 days. Only partly true at Sampada, where compliance review (6.5 days), code review (7.1) and the read window (20) are all substantial. When three stages are within a factor of two of each other, Goldratt's advice to elevate the single constraint produces an oscillation: you fix one, another binds, you fix that, the first returns. Reinertsen's advice — reduce batch size and variability everywhere — is the better fit in that regime.

Claim three: cycle time is economically meaningful. This is the claim most often assumed rather than tested. It is strongly true for Sampada's growth experiments, where a four-week read window directly limits the number of learning cycles per year: 38-day cycles allow about 9 sequential learnings a year, 25-day cycles allow 14, and for a team whose value comes from compounding small wins that is a 50% increase in the rate of improvement. It is weakly true for Neelambar's enterprise contracts, where the customer's procurement calendar means that shipping three weeks earlier changes revenue recognition not at all.

Claim four: the work in the pipeline is worth doing. If it is not, shortening the cycle increases the rate at which you produce waste. This is not a rhetorical caution: at Sampada, four of the eleven planned launches had been committed in an annual planning round nine months earlier and had no evidence behind them stronger than a competitive screenshot.

The frame is actively misleading in three situations. First, when the true constraint is demand-side — the organisation does not know what to build — flow analysis produces a confident, quantitative answer to the wrong question, and the resulting investment makes the real problem harder to see because everyone is now busy. Second, in genuinely exploratory work, where rework is the point; measuring the cycle time of a research spike and driving it down selects for shallow exploration. Third, when the cycle contains a mandatory external party — a regulator, an auditor, a customer's security team — whose duration is contractual. There, "elevating the constraint" means renegotiating a contract, which is a commercial move, not an engineering one, and pretending otherwise wastes a quarter.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product organisations. When several product teams depend on one platform or one shared service — identity, payments, the data pipeline — the shared team is a single server serving many arrival streams, and Kingman's formula applies to it directly. Sampada's compliance function was exactly this: two people reviewing every change that touched risk profiling, suitability language or fee disclosure, for four product teams. Arrivals quadrupled with AI tooling; the function did not grow. Mature companies handle this in one of two ways that they rarely describe accurately in public. The stated approach is "we embedded compliance into the teams." The actual approach is usually a classification rule that removes 80% of changes from the queue altogether — a documented list of change types that are pre-approved — leaving the specialists to handle the 20% that genuinely require judgement. The rule, not the embedding, is what moves the number.

Two-sided marketplaces. Neelambar's carrier marketplace created a structural asymmetry: shipper-side changes could be ramped by cohort, but carrier-side changes to rate cards or acceptance flows had to go to all carriers at once in a region, because carriers compare notes and a partial rollout produces accusations of discrimination. That converts the rollout stage from a continuously variable dial into a binary event with a much higher approval bar, which lengthens the decision stage upstream. The general pattern: any constraint on how you can roll out propagates backwards into how carefully you must decide.

Regulated products. Sampada operated under SEBI's investment-adviser and distributor regimes and under the DPDP Act for personal data. The relevant mechanic is not that review is slow but that review is serialised and non-delegable: a qualified person must sign, and that person cannot be duplicated by tooling. The honest treatment is to model regulatory review as a fixed-capacity server and to manage its arrival stream — through change classification, through batching related changes into a single reviewable submission, and through pre-clearing patterns rather than instances.

Hardware plus software. Where firmware or a device is involved, the release stage has a floor set by physics and certification rather than by process. A team shipping to an electric two-wheeler fleet or a payment terminal has an over-the-air update cadence measured in weeks and a certification step measured in months; generation speed is essentially irrelevant to time-to-customer, and the only meaningful flow work is on the decision stage, where committing to the wrong thing costs a full hardware cycle.

AI-native products. This is the case that inverts the usual pattern. When the product itself contains a model, verification does not merely fail to get cheaper — it gets more expensive, because behaviour is non-deterministic and a change can regress quality in ways no unit test catches. The verification stage becomes an evaluation stage: a suite of graded examples, a held-out set, a human review panel for a sample of outputs. Sampada's goal-planning assistant, which explained fund selections in plain language, required a 400-example evaluation reviewed by two certified advisers before any prompt or model change went live, and that review took four to six working days regardless of how small the change was. For AI-native teams the velocity illusion is at its most acute, because generation is at its cheapest and verification at its most expensive.

At the organisational seams. The general result across all these cases is that time accumulates wherever ownership changes. Figure 2 makes the point: every arrow between two differently-managed boxes is a queue, and no individual manager's dashboard shows it.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

An expert distrusts an improvement that arrives without a corresponding worsening

Conservation is the default assumption: if build fell five days and the cycle fell five days, either something genuinely structural changed or the measurement window excludes the stage that absorbed it. The tell is a cycle-time definition whose last timestamp is a deploy. Ask what happens to a change in the fortnight after deployment; if the answer involves a flag, a customer communication or a metric, the measurement is incomplete.

They distinguish wait time from touch time inside every stage before proposing anything

The obvious reading of a six-day review stage is "reviewers are slow". The expert reading is that six days of elapsed time containing twenty minutes of reading is a scheduling problem, and six days containing five hours of reading is a comprehension problem caused by change size. The remedies — a review rota with a same-day service level versus a hard cap on diff size — share nothing.

They watch the second derivative: which queue is growing, not which is largest

The largest queue today is often one that has already been noticed and is being worked. The queue that will bind next quarter is the one whose length is increasing. At Neelambar the largest stage was customer UAT at eleven days, but the growing one was internal verification, up from 2.4 to 4.1 days across two quarters, because generated changes touched more modules and therefore triggered more of the regression suite.

They treat utilisation targets as policy, not as an outcome

A competent practitioner reports that reviewers are at 84% utilisation. An expert sets 75% as a target and staffs to it, because they know the waiting-time curve and know that the last ten points of utilisation buy a few hours of engineer time and cost several days of calendar time. This is the single hardest idea to sell upward, because deliberate slack looks like waste in every capacity plan ever written.

They know which stages are calendars and stop trying to optimise them

The tell is a stage whose duration is suspiciously stable across very different items — Neelambar's five-day wait for the customer's alternate-Monday scheduling window never varied by change size. A stage with near-zero variance is almost always a calendar. You move it by moving the calendar or by decoupling from it, never by working harder.

They read the change-failure rate alongside every speed metric

Any speed improvement should be presented with its stability counterpart. An expert regards a fall in review time accompanied by a rise in change-failure rate as a transfer of work from a visible stage to an invisible one, not as a win, and can usually name the size of the transfer: at Sampada, change-failure rate rose from 8% to 19%, and at 26 deploys a week that is roughly 2.9 extra failures weekly, each consuming about four senior-engineer hours — about twelve hours a week removed from the review pool, which is itself a measurable fraction of the capacity shortfall.

They separate the rate of learning from the rate of shipping

The economically interesting quantity for a growth team is learnings per year, not launches per year, and the two diverge sharply when the read window dominates. An expert will happily accept a longer build in exchange for an experiment design that yields a readable result three weeks sooner, because the read stage is where the calendar actually sits.

They are suspicious of their own team's self-report

Given the reproducible finding that perceived speed-ups exceed measured ones, an expert treats engineer sentiment as a measure of friction and morale — both real and worth managing — and never as a measure of cycle time. The tell in a meeting is the phrase "it feels much faster now", offered in place of a number.

They ask who is inside the cycle who does not work here

Enterprise and regulated products routinely have external parties in the critical path, and internal flow programmes systematically ignore them because they cannot be tasked. Dev's largest single lever was a contract clause, not a tool.

They know the bottleneck will move and plan the sequence in advance

A competent practitioner solves the current constraint. An expert names the next two before starting, because the sequence determines whether the first fix delivers any calendar benefit at all. Relieving review at Sampada while leaving a fortnightly release train in place would convert a six-day queue into a six-day wait for the train and show zero improvement, which would then be read organisationally as evidence that flow work does not pay.

7. How this plays out across product types and stages

In consumer products the constraint after build almost always migrates to the read stage, for the arithmetic reason given earlier: statistical power is bought with traffic and time, and neither is affected by generation speed. The corollary is that consumer teams gain most from increasing experiment concurrency — the number of non-interfering tests a surface can carry — rather than from shortening any single stage.

In B2B and enterprise the constraint migrates outward, into the customer's organisation: security review, sandbox validation, change-advisory boards, contractual release windows. Neelambar's case is typical, and the remedies are commercial and architectural rather than procedural — feature flags that let a customer opt in on their own schedule, a decoupled release model where the customer's acceptance applies to a configuration rather than to a build.

In platforms and marketplaces the constraint is usually a shared internal service with many arrival streams, and the highest-leverage intervention is a classification rule that removes most traffic from the specialist queue.

In hardware-plus-software the software cycle is simply subordinate to the hardware calendar, and flow work on the software side has little effect on time-to-customer. Say this plainly rather than producing a flow programme that cannot pay back.

In AI products, as discussed, verification inflates rather than deflates, and the evaluation suite becomes the constraint almost immediately.

By stage: in a company under about thirty people, decision cost is near zero, read is near useless for lack of traffic, and generation speed genuinely does compress the calendar — this is the population that reports the largest and most credible gains. Between thirty and three hundred, the decision and review stages inflate faster than anything else, and this is where velocity illusions are most common and most damaging, because the organisation still remembers being fast. Above a thousand, decision and rollout together commonly account for two-thirds of cycle time, generation speed is nearly irrelevant to delivery speed, and the honest framing of AI tooling's benefit is engineer capacity and morale rather than time-to-market. One difference that is often asserted and is not real: the claim that regulated industries are inherently slower. Measured per stage, their review stages are comparable; what differs is that their calendars are contractual and therefore unmovable by internal effort.

8. Three worked examples

Example one: Sampada relieves the wrong stage first

In October 2025 Sampada had already run this play once, and it failed. The team observed a review queue of 7.1 days, hired three senior engineers at a fully loaded ₹68 lakh a year each, and assigned them primarily to review. Arrivals, however, rose with them: the three new engineers also wrote changes, adding roughly 9 PRs a week to an existing 79. Capacity rose from about 105 to 128 reviews a week; arrivals rose from 79 to 88. Utilisation fell from 0.75 to 0.69, and predicted wait fell from about 3.0 service times to 2.2 — a real improvement of roughly 1.2 days. But the fortnightly release train, at a five-day average wait, absorbed it entirely. The measured cycle time moved from 38.4 to 38.1 days. The organisation had spent ₹2.04 crore annually for three-tenths of a day, and — this was the expensive part — concluded that flow analysis did not work. The recovery took a quarter and began with Rhea re-running the measurement with wait and touch separated per stage, which showed that of the 7.1 review days, 6.3 were waiting; that capacity had fallen because median diff size had grown 86%; and that the release train was now the binding calendar. The corrected sequence was a 200-line diff cap first, the release train moved to weekly second, and no hiring.

Example three: the AI-native inversion at Sampada's goal assistant

Sampada's goal-planning assistant produced plain-language explanations of fund recommendations. Before AI tooling, a copy or logic change took 4 days to build and 1 day to verify. After, it took 0.5 days to build and 5.5 days to verify, because the change now had to pass a 400-example evaluation graded on factual accuracy, suitability language and the absence of anything resembling a return guarantee, with two certified advisers reviewing the 40 lowest-scoring outputs. Total stage time went from 5.0 days to 6.0. Generation got eight times cheaper and the stage got slower. The recovery here was not to weaken the evaluation but to change its granularity: Sampada built a 60-example smoke set that ran in twenty minutes and gated only the full suite on changes that moved smoke-set scores, which returned the median to 2.8 days while leaving the adviser review in place for the changes that actually needed it.

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs and the cost of late detection

Reporting throughput as speed. Early sign: a velocity slide made entirely of counts. Diagnostic question: what is the median and 85th-percentile number of days from commitment to customer availability, for the last forty completed items? Caught late, the cost is a full planning cycle committed on a false productivity multiplier — Dev's CEO was one meeting away from committing 40% more 2026 scope on exactly this basis.

Adding capacity at a non-constraint. Early sign: growth in the count of items that are finished but not released. Diagnostic question: at which stage is the number of waiting items increasing week on week? Cost of lateness: Sampada's ₹2.04 crore, plus the harder-to-price organisational conclusion that the method does not work.

Relieving review by lowering the bar. Early sign: review time and change-failure rate moving in opposite directions in the same period. Diagnostic question: has the share of approvals with no comments risen? Caught late, the cost arrives as an incident in a regulated surface, where the expense is not the outage but the reporting obligation.

Batch growth. Early sign: median diff size rising while PR count rises, which is the specific signature of cheap generation. Diagnostic question: what is the distribution of change size this quarter versus a year ago? Late cost: review capacity silently halves and everyone blames the reviewers.

Measuring the tool instead of the system. Early sign: a dashboard of assistant acceptance rates and percentage-of-code-generated. Diagnostic question: what customer-visible quantity changes if this number doubles? Late cost: two years of investment justified by a metric that cannot fail.

Optimising a calendar. Early sign: a stage whose duration has near-zero variance across very different items. Diagnostic question: what determines when this stage starts? Late cost: a quarter of process work with no calendar movement.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is there one constraint or many? The constraint school holds that at any moment one stage binds and everything else is noise; the evidence is decades of manufacturing practice and the repeated experience that focused interventions outperform broad ones. The queueing school holds that product development has high variability and many near-critical stages, so that the "constraint" flickers between them week to week and a single-constraint model produces whack-a-mole; the evidence is the variance structure of real cycle-time data, where stage rankings are unstable across quarters. What would have to be true for the constraint school to be wrong: stage durations would have to be so variable that the identity of the slowest stage changes faster than an intervention can be implemented. That is an empirical question a team can answer with its own data in an afternoon, and the answer differs by organisation — which is why both schools have honest adherents.

Do flow metrics belong in front of executives? One camp argues they must be, because otherwise leadership reasons about capacity using output counts and makes exactly Dev's CEO's error. The other argues that any metric shown to executives is eventually gamed, and that cycle time is unusually easy to game — by redefining the start timestamp, by splitting items, by excluding hard classes of work. Both are right about their failure mode, and the disagreement is really about which failure is cheaper in a given culture.

Does AI tooling actually shorten delivery at all? The optimistic position rests on large observed reductions in time-to-first-draft and on the real experience of teams in greenfield or boilerplate-heavy work; the sceptical position rests on controlled studies where measured completion time did not improve, or worsened, in complex familiar codebases, and on the consistent gap between perceived and measured gains. The honest synthesis is narrower than either camp would like: the effect is large and real at the build stage, is highly context-dependent, and translates into delivery time only in proportion to the build stage's share of the cycle — which in most organisations above a hundred people is under a quarter.

Is review a cost or a product? One position treats review as pure overhead to be minimised, ideally by automating it. The other treats review as the stage where an organisation's understanding of its own system is maintained, and argues that a team which stops reading its code loses the ability to make good decisions about it within about two years — a cost that appears in the decision stage, not the review stage, and therefore never shows up in the analysis that justified removing the review. Nobody has good longitudinal data on this yet, and it is probably the most consequential open question in the field.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a dashboard. Someone who has internalised it arrives with a sequence and a set of policies. They can state, from memory, which stage currently binds, which will bind next, and the arithmetic that says so. They set batch-size and utilisation policy rather than exhorting people to be faster, because they know that policy changes the shape of the queue and exhortation changes only the mood of the queue. They present every speed number with its stability counterpart, refuse to accept "it feels faster" as evidence, and are entirely comfortable saying that a proposed improvement will produce no calendar benefit — the sentence that most distinguishes them, because it costs political capital and prevents the expensive failure in Example one. They treat the external parties inside their cycle as negotiable, and take a contract to the commercial team rather than a process to the engineering team when the numbers point there. And they keep the question open that the numbers cannot answer: whether the things moving through this faster pipe are worth moving at all.

12. What Rhea and Dev decided

Rhea's answer to the board member's marginal note was that the five days had gone into the review queue, the compliance queue and the release train, in roughly the proportions 2.4, 1.1 and 1.5, and that she could show the timestamps. Her proposal was a sequence with a number attached to each element: a 200-line diff cap, a change-classification rule that pre-cleared 70% of changes from compliance review, and a move from a fortnightly to a weekly release train. Predicted effect, 9.4 days off a 38-day median. She declined to commit to more launches in 2026 and committed instead to more readable experiments: 14 sequential learning cycles against the prior year's 9. Her reasoning was that Sampada's advantage came from compounding small improvements to the goal-planning funnel, and that the rate of compounding, not the count of launches, was the quantity the board should track.

Dev told his CEO that he would accept 40% more scope on internal and configuration work, where the cycle was genuinely 30% shorter, and would not accept it on customer-visible workflow changes, where the cycle had moved 1.3 days in a year. He asked for three things: three weeks of engineering on customer-controlled flags, the sales head's time to renegotiate the delivery-versus-enablement clause with the Dubai forwarder, and permission to make the regression suite selective. He described the request in one sentence at the end of his memo: we have made the cheapest part of the process cheaper, and the expensive parts are now in other people's calendars.

Discussion questions.

1. Sampada's first attempt — hiring three engineers into the review queue — was defensible on the data available in October 2025. What specific additional measurement would have prevented it, and why was that measurement not taken?

2. Dev's largest single lever is a contract clause rather than an engineering change. What does that imply about who should own flow measurement in an enterprise software company, and what goes wrong when engineering owns it alone?

3. If the sceptical school is right that measured productivity gains from AI tooling are much smaller than perceived ones, what should Rhea tell her engineers — who are, by every survey, considerably happier — and how should that shape what she reports to the board?

13. Going deeper

Reviewing work you did not write — the craft of the stage that most often becomes the new constraint; it determines whether relieving the queue costs you quality. AI-native teams — the organisational forms in which this throughput-without-cycle-time pattern shows up first and most sharply. Outputs vs outcomes vs impact — the discipline that stops a shortened cycle from delivering irrelevant work sooner, and the reason Claim four above is not rhetorical. Roadmaps when build time collapses — what a plan looks like when build estimates are no longer the binding input to sequencing. Which PM skills repriced, up and down — the labour-market consequence of the same shift, and where a PM's time is now worth most. Decision speed versus decision quality — the tension that appears immediately once the decision stage becomes the constraint. When building gets cheap and deciding does not — the general economic statement of which this topic is the measurement practice. Discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn't — the same asymmetry applied upstream of the build. The prototype as the new specification — one of the few interventions that genuinely shortens the decision stage rather than the build. What a PRD becomes when the reader can build — the document-level consequence. Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill — what becomes valuable when generation is abundant and review is the constraint. Analytics when anyone can query the data — the same illusion in the measurement function, where query volume rises and decision quality does not.

Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved

The question this page answers: we are shipping faster than ever, so why isn't anything moving faster?

1. Two hundred and eleven pull requests

On Thursday, 6 November 2025, Meera Raghunathan sat in a room on the third floor of Vartalaap Cloud's office in Koramangala, Bengaluru, looking at a chart she had asked for and now wished she had not. Vartalaap sold a customer-conversation platform — a shared inbox that merged email, WhatsApp Business, voice and in-app chat — to mid-market Indian companies: pharmacy chains, coaching institutes, appliance brands, a few insurers. It had 4,200 paying customers, ₹128 crore of annual recurring revenue, and 68 engineers split between Bengaluru and Pune. Freshworks and Zoho Desk sat above it in the market; a dozen smaller players sat below. Meera was VP Product.

The chart showed pull requests merged per week. A pull request, or PR, is a unit of proposed code change that one engineer submits and another must read and approve before it enters the product. In January 2025, before the engineering organisation standardised on AI coding assistants, Vartalaap merged a median of 34 PRs a week. By October it merged 71. Deployments to production had gone from nine a week to twenty-six. Arvind Salunke, the CTO, had opened the quarterly business review with that slide and the phrase "our velocity has doubled."

Meera's difficulty was that she had the other list. At the start of 2025 the product organisation had committed to six things for the year: a WhatsApp catalogue ordering flow, a rebuilt reporting module, an agent-assist summariser, single sign-on for enterprise buyers, an outbound campaign tool, and migration of the largest 200 accounts off the legacy routing engine. In November, two had shipped to all customers, two sat behind flags at under 10% of traffic, and two had not started. Every one of the four in flight had been "code complete" for between three and nine weeks.

Anita Iyer, the CEO, had asked a question in that QBR that Meera could not yet answer: if the engineering team is producing twice as much work, and the roadmap has not moved, where is the work going? Arvind's answer was that he needed eight more engineers, at roughly ₹1.8 crore a year fully loaded. Meera had three weeks to support that request or propose something else. Getting it wrong was expensive in either direction: hire into a constraint that is not the constraint and you have spent ₹1.8 crore to make the queue longer.

2. The idea, stated precisely

A velocity illusion is the gap between the speed at which a team produces work and the speed at which the organisation converts an idea into an outcome for a customer. The first has become dramatically cheaper; the second is governed by whatever stage now runs slowest. When the two are confused, a team can double its output, feel faster, report faster, and deliver no sooner.

Three definitions make the rest of this page readable. Throughput is how many items finish per unit of time — 71 PRs a week. Cycle time is how long one item takes to travel from the moment somebody commits to it until it is in customers' hands and its effect is known. Flow efficiency is the fraction of that cycle time during which somebody was actually working on the item rather than it sitting in a queue. Organisations that measure flow efficiency honestly usually find it between 5% and 20%, and that single number is the whole argument: if work is being touched 15% of the time, making the touching five times faster changes the calendar very little. Managers are trained to keep people busy, which is resource efficiency; customers experience flow efficiency, and the two are in direct tension.

The intellectual lineage is older than AI. Eliyahu Goldratt's The Goal (1984) set out the Theory of Constraints: in any system of dependent steps, output is set by the slowest step, and improvement anywhere else is an illusion of progress. Donald Reinertsen's The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) applied queueing theory to product work and showed that in knowledge work the queues are invisible — nobody sees a pile of half-finished decisions the way they see a pile of half-finished castings. Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim's Accelerate (2018) gave software teams the DORA measures, of which the relevant pair is deployment frequency, a throughput measure, and lead time for change, a cycle-time measure. Generative coding assistants did not create the problem; they made the gap between those two measures wide enough that anyone could see it.

The sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "Writing the code was about a quarter of our calendar time, so making it five times faster can improve our delivery by at most a quarter — and only if nothing downstream gets worse. Let me show you where the other three quarters sit."

3. How the measurement actually works

The method has four steps, and practitioners routinely skip the first and the last.

Step one: define the cycle you actually care about, end to end. Most engineering tools measure from first commit to production deploy. That window excludes the two stages where product organisations lose most of their time: the decision that precedes the work, and the rollout and learning that follow it. Meera defined Vartalaap's cycle as running from the day a change was accepted into the plan to the day it was serving 100% of eligible customers and its primary metric had been read. That definition is arguable; what matters is that it is written down and applied consistently, because every comparison here is a before-and-after on the same definition.

Step two: cut the cycle into stages with observable boundaries. A stage boundary must be a timestamp something already records, or one you can start recording this week. Vartalaap used six: decision-to-start, build, review, verification, release-wait, and rollout-and-read. Anything you cannot timestamp becomes invisible, and invisible time is exactly the time that grows.

Step three: measure elapsed time per stage per item, and look at the distribution. Elapsed calendar time, not effort. If a PR is opened on Friday at 6 p.m. and reviewed on Monday at 11 a.m., the review stage cost 2.7 days even though the reviewing took twenty minutes. Report the median and the 85th percentile: the first tells you the typical experience, the second tells you what the sales team is complaining about.

Step four: find the stage that absorbed the released time, and the stage whose queue is growing. These are usually the same stage, but not always. A stage can be slow because it is genuinely hard, or slow because a queue has formed in front of it, and the remedies differ: capacity and batch size for queues, redesign for hard work, calendar surgery for fixed-cadence stages such as a fortnightly release train, where the average wait is half the interval no matter how fast anyone works.

4. The arithmetic, worked line by line

Meera pulled two quarters of data: 61 changes that completed their cycle in Q1 2025 and 94 that completed in Q3. For each she had six timestamps. Table 1 is the median elapsed time per stage.

Table 1. Vartalaap Cloud: median working days per stage, per completed change.

Read the table as an accounting identity. Build fell 72%, from 6.5 days to 1.8. Every day of that saving, and a little more, reappeared downstream: review gained 3.5 days, verification 1.5. Throughput genuinely doubled and the delivery calendar moved three-tenths of a day in the wrong direction.

Before diagnosing why, establish the ceiling. Build was 6.5 of 27.0 days, or 24% of the cycle. Suppose the assistants had been perfect and build had fallen to zero, with nothing downstream changing. The cycle would be 20.5 days — an improvement of 24%, and not a day more. This is Amdahl's Law: the speed-up available from improving one part of a system is capped by the share of time that part occupied. If a stage is fraction f of the total and you make it k times faster, overall speed-up is 1 ÷ ((1−f) + f/k). With f = 0.24 and k = 3.6, that is 1 ÷ (0.76 + 0.067) = 1.21, a 21% improvement. Vartalaap got nothing, so something else changed.

The something else is a queue. Review is a service: work arrives at some rate, and reviewers clear it at some rate. Utilisation, written ρ, is arrival rate divided by capacity, and standard queueing results say expected waiting time scales as ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) times the service time — a curve nearly flat until it is nearly vertical. Vartalaap's fourteen senior reviewers spent about ninety minutes a day reviewing, and a typical Q1 PR took roughly forty-five minutes, giving capacity of about 28 reviews a day, or 140 a week. Reviewers cleared their queue once a working day, so treat one day as the service unit.

Two things deserve attention. First, capacity fell from 140 to 86 a week even though no reviewer left. It fell because the median PR grew from 190 lines to 340: when writing is cheap, people write more per submission, and review effort rises faster than line count because a reviewer must hold the whole change in their head. Second, the model under-predicts the observed wait by about two days in Q1 and one in Q3. That should be said out loud: the formula assumes random arrivals and a single pooled server, and Vartalaap's reviews cluster on specific specialists. The model is not a forecast; its value is the shape. It says that between ρ = 0.24 and ρ = 0.83 waiting should rise roughly fifteen-fold, and the data agree that something non-linear happened.

The second pass: change one input. The third column of Table 2 holds arrivals fixed at 71 a week — nobody writes less — and reduces median PR size to 120 lines by requiring changes to be split. Capacity rises to 190, ρ falls to 0.37, predicted wait falls to 0.6 days. Applying the same two-day model-to-reality gap that Q1 showed, review lands near 2.6 days, and the full cycle falls from 27.3 to roughly 23.9 days.

Now look at what that leaves: rollout and read at 6.0 days, release wait at 5.0, verification 4.5, decision 4.0. The constraint has moved from review to the release train — a stage where no amount of individual effort helps, because a fortnightly train imposes an average wait of half its interval by construction. That is the central discipline of this topic. Finding the bottleneck is not a project with an end; it is a loop you re-run every quarter, because relieving one stage promotes another.

5. The nuances a learner must acquire

Throughput and cycle time are different quantities, and Little's Law ties them together

Little's Law states that average work in progress equals average throughput multiplied by average cycle time. At Vartalaap, throughput doubled and cycle time held, so work in progress doubled: twice as many half-finished things sitting in the system at any moment. That is not a neutral fact. Every item in progress consumes context, invites status meetings, and ages — and code that has been waiting three weeks for review needs rebasing, which creates new work. High WIP is both a symptom of a downstream constraint and a cause of further slowdown.

Some stages are queues, some are hard work, and some are calendars

The three need different remedies and are easily confused. A queue responds to capacity and batch size; hard work responds to redesign, tooling or scope reduction; a calendar — a release train, an architecture review board, a client's change-freeze window — responds only to changing the calendar. Vartalaap's largest banking customers had contractual change windows of one weekend a month, putting an irreducible fourteen-day average into the rollout stage for those accounts. No engineering investment would have touched it.

Faster generation can make the cycle longer, not merely fail to shorten it

Three mechanisms do this, and all three appeared at Vartalaap. Batch sizes grow, because the cost of writing more is now low. Review quality degrades under load, so defects escape and return as rework later in the cycle. And reviewing work nobody on the team wrote takes longer per line than reviewing a colleague's work, because the reviewer cannot rely on knowing how the author thinks. Vartalaap's change-failure rate — the share of deployments needing a fix or rollback — rose from 9% to 17% between Q1 and Q3, and each of those incidents consumed reviewer attention, which was the scarce resource.

The median hides the cases that cost you the contract

Vartalaap's median cycle was 27.3 days; its 85th percentile was 61 days, and the features in that tail were disproportionately the enterprise ones — single sign-on, the routing migration — because they involved security review, the customer's own testing window and cross-team dependencies. If the business pain is concentrated in a tail, a median-based bottleneck hunt points at the wrong stage.

You cannot infer the counterfactual from a before-and-after

Between January and October, Vartalaap also grew from 54 to 68 engineers, acquired two accounts with heavier compliance demands, and moved its release train from weekly to fortnightly for stability reasons. The honest claim is not "AI assistants caused our cycle time to stall"; it is "our cycle time did not improve, and here is the stage-level accounting of where the time sits". The second claim is enough to act on and needs no causal story you cannot support.

What this analysis cannot tell you

It is silent on whether the work was worth doing. A team can shorten its cycle from 27 days to 12 and produce nothing customers value; done well, a bottleneck analysis simply makes a badly-prioritised roadmap fail faster and more visibly. Before relying on the method, a newcomer should ask three questions: what are the boundaries of the cycle we measure, who chose them, and what would show up as improvement that is not?

6. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the constraint after build usually sits in the learning stage rather than the approval stage. A consumer team can deploy in an hour, but if a change needs an A/B test with enough traffic to detect a 2% lift, the calendar is set by arithmetic no assistant can shorten: at 60,000 daily eligible users and a baseline conversion of 8%, detecting a 2% relative lift at conventional power takes about three weeks of exposure. Build time falling to zero leaves those three weeks intact, which is why consumer teams that adopt AI tooling often discover their constraint is experiment capacity — the number of concurrent tests a surface can carry without interference.

In B2B and enterprise software, Vartalaap's world, the constraint migrates to verification and to the buyer's own calendar: security questionnaires, sandbox validation, change-advisory boards, contractual release windows. The customer sits inside your cycle time and you do not control them. In marketplaces the distinctive constraint is that changes must be safe for two populations at once — a pricing change that helps buyers can be an emergency for sellers — so rollouts stage by cohort and the read stage lengthens because the two sides respond on different timescales.

Stage matters as much as type. In a fifteen-person company the decision stage is nearly free and the read stage nearly useless for want of traffic; the constraint is the founder's attention, and AI-assisted generation genuinely does compress the calendar. At Vartalaap's size the decision stage has itself become expensive. In a large enterprise, decision and rollout together routinely account for two-thirds of the cycle, at which point build speed is close to irrelevant to delivery and highly relevant to morale.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting throughput as though it were speed

The symptom, visible from outside, is a leadership deck whose velocity slide shows counts — deploys, PRs, story points — and never a distribution of elapsed times. The misunderstanding is treating a rate as a duration. The diagnostic: ask for the histogram of days from commitment to customer availability for the last forty completed items. If nobody can produce it in a week, the absence is itself the finding.

Hiring into the wrong stage

The symptom is a request for engineers when the backlog of finished-but-unreleased work is growing. Arvind's eight engineers would have raised arrivals at review from 71 a week to roughly 88, pushing ρ above 1.0, at which point queueing theory stops giving you a number and starts giving you an unbounded backlog. The diagnostic is one question: at which stage is the number of waiting items growing week on week? Add capacity there or nowhere.

Relieving the review queue by lowering the bar

This is the most dangerous mistake because it works for about six weeks. The symptom is review time falling while change-failure rate and time-to-restore both rise; the underlying misunderstanding is that review is a cost rather than a verification stage whose output is confidence. The diagnostic is to track review time and change-failure rate on the same chart, and to treat any improvement in one accompanied by deterioration in the other as a transfer, not a gain.

Measuring the tool instead of the system

The symptom is a dashboard of assistant-acceptance rates and percentage-of-code-generated. These measure adoption of a tool, which is an input. They cannot distinguish a team that has genuinely compressed its calendar from one that has merely moved its labour from typing to reviewing. The diagnostic: for any proposed AI metric, ask what customer-visible quantity would change if the metric doubled. If no answer survives thirty seconds, it is an input metric wearing an outcome's clothes.

8. What good looks like

A product organisation that has internalised this keeps one chart on a wall: median and 85th-percentile days per stage, updated monthly, with the constraint stage marked. It names one constraint at a time and refuses to fund improvements elsewhere until that one has moved, because improvements elsewhere are by construction invisible. It sets policy at the batch level rather than the effort level — a hard limit on PR size, a limit on concurrent work in progress, a rule that nothing enters the plan until the previous item has cleared rollout. It reports throughput and cycle time side by side and treats a divergence between them as a finding rather than a nuisance. And when a stage is a calendar rather than a queue, it goes after the calendar: moving from a fortnightly train to a weekly one halves the average wait at that stage, a larger and cheaper win than any amount of individual heroism.

9. What Meera decided

Meera did not support the hiring request, and did not oppose it on principle. She proposed a ninety-day sequence with a measurement attached to each step: a hard limit of 150 changed lines per pull request, aimed at review, worth 3 to 3.5 days by Table 2; a move from a fortnightly release train to a weekly one, worth 2.5 days by arithmetic alone; and a rollout runbook with a default seven-day ramp, aimed at the four features sitting behind flags because nobody owned the decision to widen them. Her commitment to Anita was a median cycle of 20 days by the end of Q1 2026, measured on the same six stages, with the hiring question revisited then on evidence rather than on the shape of the backlog. Her reasoning fitted in a line: the constraint is not the number of hands, it is the number of things waiting for a small number of eyes, and adding hands makes that worse before it makes it better.

What to learn next. Reviewing work you did not write is the immediate sequel, because review is where the constraint sat and the craft of reviewing generated work differs from reviewing a colleague's. Outputs versus outcomes versus impact stops a shortened cycle from merely delivering irrelevant work sooner. And roadmaps when build time collapses follows: if build is no longer the scarce input, a plan shaped around build estimates is the wrong shape.

Two questions to sit with.

1. In your own organisation, what is the last timestamp in the cycle you currently measure — and what happens to an idea after that timestamp that customers would count as part of the wait?

2. If your team's generation speed tripled tomorrow and your delivery calendar did not move at all, which stage would have absorbed the time — and could you prove it with data you already have?

Saras Insure Cloud: sixty-three days

Two dashboards in the same company describe the same year. One says the engineering organisation is among the fastest Ananya Bhatt has ever run. The other says nothing has reached a customer any sooner than it did in 2019.

1. Sunday night, 8 February 2026

The memo was due in the board's pre-read folder by nine on Monday morning. Ananya Bhatt had been writing it since Friday and had four versions, none of which she believed.

She was at her desk at home in Bandra, Mumbai, with the Arabian Sea somewhere beyond the building opposite and a printout of two spreadsheets in front of her. The board of Saras Insure Cloud met on Thursday 12 February to approve a ₹4.5 crore capacity investment and to confirm — or revise — the eighteen deliverables the CEO had committed to for calendar 2026. Ananya, co-founder and Chief Product Officer, had to recommend where the money went and whether the eighteen were real.

The difficulty was that she could make an honest, evidence-backed case for three incompatible answers, and she had received, in the past ten days, a memo from Toronto, a legal note from Singapore, a hiring plan from Bengaluru and a design manifesto from Berlin, each of which contradicted at least one of the others. At 11.40 p.m. she wrote a sentence at the top of a blank document — we are producing more than we ever have and delivering no faster than we did seven years ago — and then could not decide whether it was the finding or the excuse.

2. How Saras got here

Saras Insure Cloud was founded in Pune in 2016 by Ananya Bhatt and Vikram Nadkarni, who had spent six years together building claims systems inside a large Indian IT services firm and had grown tired of watching insurers pay for eighteen-month implementations. Their proposition was narrower and faster: a policy-administration and claims platform, built for the Indian general-insurance market, that could be live in twelve weeks.

By February 2026 Saras had ₹168 crore of annual recurring revenue. Its products were Saras Policy, which administered motor, health and travel policies; Saras Claims, which handled first notice of loss, document intake, adjudication support and settlement; and Saras Verify, launched in pilot in April 2025, a layer that used document-extraction and triage models to read hospital bills, discharge summaries, garage estimates and surveyor reports, and to route claims by predicted complexity. Its customers were nine Indian general insurers, forty-three brokers and managing general agents, and, since 2024, two international accounts — the most significant being Rawdah Insurance Services in Dubai, a composite broker and third-party administrator serving the UAE and Oman, worth ₹14 crore a year.

One decision from 2021 shaped everything Ananya could now consider. To win Ashwini General Insurance — then Saras's largest prospect, now its largest customer at ₹31 crore a year — Saras had agreed to a single-tenant, version-pinned deployment: Ashwini would run its own dedicated instance, would approve every upgrade in advance, and would validate each release in its own staging environment before it reached production. The clause had been drafted in a week, under deadline, and had then been offered to every subsequent enterprise customer because it was easier to reuse a contract than to negotiate a new one. By 2026, seven of the nine insurers ran their own instances on their own version calendars, and shipping a change to all of them meant nine deployments, nine change summaries, and between six and twenty working days of customer-side user-acceptance testing each.

Inside Saras this arrangement was universally believed to be a regulatory requirement. It was not. Vikram had conceded it commercially in 2021; nothing in IRDAI's guidance then or since required a dedicated instance, only a documented, auditable change-management process with named approvers. Vikram knew this. He had not corrected the belief, partly because the correction implicated a decision he had made and partly because, as he put it to himself, the customers would want it anyway.

3. The industry

Indian general insurance in 2026 was growing and consolidating at the same time. Digital-first insurers such as Acko and Go Digit had reset expectations for how quickly a motor policy could be issued; Policybazaar had reset expectations for how transparently it could be compared; and the incumbent private insurers had responded by rebuilding their claims journeys, which is where Saras made its money. The National Health Claims Exchange, built under the National Health Authority's digital health mission, was progressively standardising the exchange of health-claim documents between hospitals, insurers and TPAs, and every one of Saras's health customers had an NHCX integration on its 2026 plan. IRDAI's Bima Sugam marketplace initiative promised further standardisation and further integration work.

The regulatory perimeter mattered in three concrete ways. IRDAI's information and cyber-security guidelines required insurers to maintain documented change management with named approvers and retained evidence, which meant any change Saras shipped into a customer's instance had to arrive with an auditable trail. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the rules that followed it imposed consent, retention and breach-notification duties on the processing of claimants' health data, and Saras, as a data processor for its insurer customers, carried contractual obligations that flowed down from each of them. And GST invoicing rules governed how Saras's own settlement outputs were formatted, which sounded trivial and had twice consumed a quarter.

Competitively, Saras sat between two kinds of rival. Above it were the platform practices of the large Indian services firms, which could promise anything and take two years. Beside it were a handful of well-funded insurtech platforms, one of which had raised at a valuation Saras's board mentioned often. Below it, and increasingly relevant, were insurers' own internal teams, newly confident that AI tooling made building in-house viable. Derek Falzon, Saras's SVP Sales in New Jersey, had been selling into US managing general agents since 2024 with modest success and considerable noise.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence matters, because at each point the company believed something that later turned out to be partly wrong.

In January 2025 Saras rolled AI coding assistants out to all 112 engineers, at a licence cost of ₹68 lakh a year. Adoption was near-universal within six weeks. By June, Meher Irani, VP Engineering in Bengaluru, was reporting that the median time from an engineer starting work on a change to that change being ready for review had fallen from 8.4 working days to 2.9 — a 65% reduction. On that basis the CEO told the board in the July meeting that Saras could commit to eighteen major deliverables in 2026 against eleven in 2025, and the board minuted it.

In September, prompted by Ananya's own unease, Dr. Saurav Mitra's data team in Toronto reconstructed the full delivery path for 138 customer-visible changes. The result, Exhibit 3, showed a median of 61 working days from plan acceptance to a change being live for the customer who had requested it — statistically indistinguishable from the 59 days the same reconstruction produced for 2019, before any of the tooling existed.

On 6 October, a change to the motor-claims depreciation logic reached Ashwini General Insurance's production instance. Over the following nine days it applied an incorrect depreciation schedule to 4,300 claims, understating settlements on about 1,900 of them by amounts between ₹1,200 and ₹41,000. Ashwini detected it through its own reconciliation, not through Saras's monitoring. Remediation, reprocessing and goodwill payments cost Saras ₹1.6 crore under its service-level terms; Ashwini notified the matter to its own compliance function; Saras's name appeared in a board paper at a customer for the first time in its history.

The immediate internal conclusion, reached within seventy-two hours and never formally revisited until January, was that generated code had entered the adjudication path without adequate scrutiny. On 3 November, Saras instituted a two-approver rule for any change touching adjudication, pricing or settlement — approximately 40% of all changes — with one approver required to be from a list of six named senior engineers. Median review time on affected changes rose from 6.2 days to 12.9.

On 14 January 2026, Saurav's root-cause review concluded that the defect had not originated in generated code at all. The faulty logic was in a configuration mapping for Ashwini's 2018 motor product, hand-written by a Saras engineer in 2022, which a generated change had merely begun to exercise for a class of claims it had never previously touched. The mapping had no test coverage. Saurav's memo said, in its second paragraph, that the November policy addressed a cause that had not been present, and that the real gap was regression coverage on tenant-specific configuration. The memo was circulated to eleven people. Nobody proposed unwinding the policy, and Rajat Sundaram, Ashwini's CIO, had cited the two-approver rule approvingly in his December quarterly review.

Meanwhile, in Dubai, Rawdah Insurance Services had been waiting since August for Arabic-language claims intake, promised for Q4 2025. On 22 January, Rawdah's contract manager wrote formally invoking the delay clause: service credits of ₹18 lakh per quarter, and a right of termination if the capability had not been delivered by 31 August 2026.

5. The people

Ananya Bhatt, co-founder and Chief Product Officer, Mumbai. Position: that the company is measuring the wrong thing and has been for a year. Incentive: she owns the 2026 commitment and will be held to it. Not saying: she signed off on the eighteen-item plan in July without asking how the productivity number had been calculated.

Vikram Nadkarni, co-founder and CTO, Pune. Position: invest ₹2.8 crore in an automated verification platform — contract tests per tenant, a regulated-change evidence pipeline, and an evaluation harness for Saras Verify — and the review and verification stages will collapse. Incentive: this is his organisation's work and his intellectual preference. Not saying: that the single-tenant model was his commercial concession in 2021, and that IRDAI never required it.

Meher Irani, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: fourteen engineers, ₹3.6 crore, or the eighteen commitments are not achievable. Incentive: her span and her ability to retain her staff. Not saying: that of the six named senior approvers, four do almost all the reviews, and two of those four are in late-stage interview processes elsewhere.

Dr. Saurav Mitra, Head of Data Science, Toronto. Position: the data already answers the question and is being ignored; the constraint is deployment and customer UAT, not anything inside engineering. Incentive: the credibility of his function. Not saying: his time study covered eleven engineers over three weeks and he privately considers the confidence interval too wide to publish.

Neelima Rao, Head of Customer Success, Singapore, covering the Gulf and South-East Asia. Position: Rawdah must be unblocked first; everything else is internal politics. Incentive: her accounts and the retention number she is paid on. Not saying: in a call on 4 December she told Rawdah's operations head that Arabic intake would be live "well before Ramadan," which she had no authority to promise.

Johan Brandt, Design Director, Berlin. By Sunday night Ananya had reduced the memo to three choices, and had written each of them out with a number attached.

Option one: fund Meher's fourteen engineers. ₹3.6 crore of the ₹4.5 crore, leaving ₹90 lakh. It answers the retention risk, which is real and near-term, and it is the only option that Derek and the CEO would both describe as ambitious. Median time to hire an experienced engineer in Bengaluru or Pune was eleven weeks, so the capacity would arrive in May at the earliest, and each new engineer would add roughly one pull request a week to a queue that Exhibit 6 shows standing at 92.

Option two: fund Vikram's verification platform. ₹2.8 crore over two quarters — per-tenant contract tests, automated generation of the change evidence that IRDAI's guidelines require, and an evaluation harness for Saras Verify's extraction models. It addresses review and internal verification, which together are 20.5 of the 65 days in Exhibit 3, and it is the only option that would let the two-approver rule be relaxed without reopening the October argument. It delivers nothing before July.

Option three: unblock Rawdah first. Roughly ₹1.1 crore to deliver Arabic-language intake by May, plus a dedicated deployment path for the Gulf. It removes ₹18 lakh a quarter of service credits and a termination right on ₹14 crore of revenue. It leaves the structural problem untouched and would be the third consecutive quarter in which Saras reorganised its plan around its loudest customer.

What she had not written down, and kept returning to, was a set of things that did not fit the three options. Exhibit 5 said the broker pool — 43 firms on one shared instance — had an enablement lag of two days against Ashwini's 28. Johan's question in the Slack thread had no good answer. Four of nine insurers were not instrumented at all, and the four were the ones on the oldest contracts, which meant Exhibit 3's medians were computed on the better half of the estate. Exhibit 3 itself showed the decision stage growing from 8 days to 11.5 while everyone argued about review. And the two-approver rule, now the single largest addition to the cycle, had been introduced to solve a problem that the January analysis said had not existed — but removing it would mean telling Rajat Sundaram, four months after an incident that cost him a board conversation, that Saras had changed its mind.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The memo was due at 9 a.m. on Monday 9 February; the board met on Thursday 12 February. The capacity budget was ₹4.5 crore for the calendar year and the CFO had made clear it would not be revisited before October.

Four constraints were not negotiable. IRDAI's cyber-security guidance required documented change management with named approvers and retained evidence for every change entering an insurer's production environment; any relaxation of review had to preserve that trail, though it did not dictate how many humans were in it. The DPDP Act work — consent artefacts, retention schedules and breach-notification tooling flowing down from insurer contracts — was committed for Q2 and consumed one and a half engineers for the year. Rawdah's clause ran service credits from 1 April 2026 and gave a termination right on 31 August. And Ashwini General's contract, the 2021 template, gave the customer approval rights over the upgrade calendar; changing the deployment model for Ashwini required Ashwini's agreement, which required Rajat Sundaram's agreement, which Neelima estimated at a three-month negotiation with an uncertain outcome.

There was one further constraint that appeared in no document. Vikram, Meher, Neelima and Derek had each, in the past fortnight, described their proposal to Ananya as the one thing that would fix the company. Whatever she recommended on Monday, three of the four would read the memo as a verdict on them.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibits 2 and 3 describe the same quarter and disagree by a factor of sixteen. What exactly does each one measure, and which of the two should appear in a board pre-read? What is lost by choosing either one alone?

2. Using Exhibit 3, calculate the largest improvement in total cycle time that could have been produced by the change in build time alone, holding every other stage at its Q1 2025 value. What does that number imply about the July 2025 commitment to eighteen deliverables?

3. Exhibit 4 contains a self-report and a time study that point in opposite directions, and Exhibit 5 is missing four of nine customers. For each, state what you would need in order to rely on it, and what you would conclude in the meantime.

4. The two-approver rule was introduced in response to a cause that the January root-cause review found was not present, and is now the largest single addition to the cycle. Rajat Sundaram values it. What are the arguments for keeping it, and what would have to be true for removing it to be responsible rather than merely faster?

5. Johan Brandt's question — why does Saras deploy nine times when the broker pool is deployed once — is not one of Ananya's three options. If the single-tenant model from 2021 is the binding constraint, what would it cost to change, who would have to agree, and what should Ananya do about the fact that a widely-held belief inside the company about why it exists is wrong?

6. It is Monday morning. Ananya has until nine o'clock. What does she write in the memo, how does she allocate the ₹4.5 crore, what does she tell the board on Thursday about the eighteen 2026 commitments — and what does she say to Meher, to Vikram, to Neelima and to Rajat Sundaram in the week that follows?

At 12.50 a.m. Ananya opened the fourth version of the memo and read her own opening line again. She had written that Saras was producing more than it ever had and delivering no faster than in 2019. It was true, and it was the least useful true sentence she had ever written, because it did not say whose fault it was, and every person who would read it on Thursday would supply that part themselves.

She thought about the brokers: forty-three firms, one instance, two days. She thought about Rajat Sundaram saying that the two-approver rule was the only answer he had. She thought about the four uninstrumented insurers and the ₹62.5 crore of revenue sitting behind them that nobody had measured, and about Meher's two seniors, and about Ramadan beginning on the eighteenth.

Outside, the traffic on the sea-facing road had thinned to almost nothing. She saved the document without changing it and went to make another cup of tea.
